q: On January 1, Year 1, Ashford Corp. granted 10,000 stock options to key employees with a grant-date fair value of $12 per option. The options cliff vest after three years of service, and no forfeitures are expected. What compensation cost should Ashford recognize for Year 1?
exp: Equity-classified awards are measured at grant-date fair value and recognized over the requisite service period: 10,000 x $12 = $120,000 / 3 = $40,000 (ASC 718-10-35). Recognizing $120,000 at grant ignores the three-year service requirement.

q: Brennan Inc. granted 20,000 options with a grant-date fair value of $9 each, cliff vesting in four years. Brennan's policy is to estimate forfeitures. At the end of Year 1, it estimated 10% would be forfeited; at the end of Year 2, it revised the estimate to 15%. What compensation cost should Brennan recognize in Year 2?
exp: Cumulative cost through Year 2 is 20,000 x 85% x $9 x 2/4 = $76,500, less Year 1 cost of 20,000 x 90% x $9 x 1/4 = $40,500, so Year 2 cost is $36,000 (a change in estimate is recognized in the period of change). The $38,250 answer applies the new estimate only to Year 2 and skips the cumulative catch-up.

q: Cortland Co. granted 30,000 options that vest in equal tranches of 10,000 at the end of each of the next three years. Each option has a grant-date fair value of $6. Cortland elects to recognize cost for graded vesting awards on an accelerated (tranche-by-tranche) basis. What compensation cost is recognized in Year 1?
exp: Each $60,000 tranche is recognized over its own vesting period: $60,000/1 + $60,000/2 + $60,000/3 = $60,000 + $30,000 + $20,000 = $110,000. The $60,000 answer is the straight-line policy, which Cortland did not elect.

q: On January 1, Year 1, Dalton Corp. granted 5,000 restricted stock units (settled in shares) when its stock price was $40. The RSUs cliff vest after four years. At the end of Year 2, Dalton's stock price was $50. What compensation cost should Dalton recognize in Year 2?
exp: Equity-classified RSUs are measured once, at grant-date fair value: 5,000 x $40 = $200,000 / 4 years = $50,000 per year, with no remeasurement for later price changes. The $62,500 answer improperly remeasures at the $50 year-end price.

q: Employees of Ellison Co. exercised 1,000 stock options with an exercise price of $25. The options had a grant-date fair value of $8 each, all of which had been recognized as compensation cost. The stock has a $1 par value. By what amount should additional paid-in capital from common stock increase on exercise?
exp: Cash of $25,000 plus the $8,000 transferred from APIC-stock options equals $33,000 of total consideration; after $1,000 to common stock at par, APIC-common stock increases $32,000. The $24,000 answer ignores the previously recognized option value.

q: On January 1, Year 1, Fairbanks Inc. granted 10,000 cash-settled stock appreciation rights that cliff vest after three years. The fair value of each SAR was $5 at December 31, Year 1 and $7 at December 31, Year 2. What compensation expense should Fairbanks recognize in Year 2?
exp: Liability awards are remeasured each period: cumulative cost at end of Year 2 is 10,000 x $7 x 2/3 = $46,667, less Year 1 cost of 10,000 x $5 x 1/3 = $16,667, giving $30,000. The $46,667 answer is the cumulative liability, not the Year 2 expense.

q: Garrison Corp. granted 12,000 options with a grant-date fair value of $10 that vest only if cumulative revenue reaches a target over three years. At the end of Year 1, achievement was probable and Garrison recognized $40,000. At the end of Year 2, achievement was no longer probable. What compensation cost should Garrison recognize in Year 2?
exp: Cost for a performance condition is recognized only if the condition is probable; when it becomes improbable, previously recognized cost is reversed, so Year 2 reflects a $40,000 credit. Recording $0 leaves cost on the books for an award not expected to vest.

q: Hanover Co. granted 9,000 options that vest only if its stock price reaches $60 within three years; the derived service period is three years. The grant-date fair value, which reflects the market condition, is $7 per option. The employees render the full three years of service, but the stock price target is never reached. What total compensation cost should Hanover recognize over the three years?
exp: Market conditions are reflected in grant-date fair value, so cost of 9,000 x $7 = $63,000 is recognized if the service is rendered, even if the market condition is never met (ASC 718-10-30-14). Reversing cost to $0 is the treatment for an unmet performance condition, not a market condition.

q: Ivers Inc. repriced 10,000 fully vested employee stock options. Immediately before the modification, the options had a fair value of $2 each; immediately after, the modified options had a fair value of $5 each. What compensation cost should Ivers recognize as a result of the repricing?
exp: A modification creates incremental cost equal to the fair value of the modified award minus the fair value of the original award immediately before modification: ($5 - $2) x 10,000 = $30,000, recognized immediately because the options are vested. The $50,000 answer ignores the value of the original award.

q: Jasper Corp.'s employee stock purchase plan lets employees buy shares at 85% of the market price on the purchase date, with no look-back feature. During the year, employees bought 2,000 shares when the market price was $40. Assuming the plan does not meet the conditions to be noncompensatory, what compensation cost should Jasper recognize?
exp: A discount above 5% generally makes an ESPP compensatory, and then the entire discount is compensation: 2,000 x $40 x 15% = $12,000 (ASC 718-50). The $8,000 answer counts only the discount in excess of 5%, which is not how the guidance works.

q: Kendall Inc. recognized $100,000 of compensation cost for nonqualified stock options this year. Kendall's tax rate is 21%, and the options are expected to generate a tax deduction when exercised. What deferred tax asset should Kendall recognize at year-end for these options?
exp: Nonqualified options normally produce a future tax deduction, so a deferred tax asset is recognized on cumulative book compensation cost: $100,000 x 21% = $21,000. $0 would be correct for incentive stock options, which ordinarily produce no deduction.

q: Lambert Co. recognized $100,000 of compensation cost and a $21,000 deferred tax asset for nonqualified options. When the options were exercised, Lambert received a tax deduction of $150,000 based on intrinsic value. The tax rate is 21%. How is the excess tax benefit recognized?
exp: The actual benefit is $150,000 x 21% = $31,500; after reversing the $21,000 DTA, the $10,500 excess benefit is recognized in income tax expense under ASU 2016-09. Crediting APIC follows the superseded pool approach.

q: Morrow Corp. granted incentive stock options and recognized $60,000 of compensation cost, with no deferred tax asset. In a later year, an employee made a disqualifying disposition that gave Morrow a $45,000 tax deduction. The tax rate is 21%. How should Morrow account for the tax effect of the disqualifying disposition?
choices: Reduce income tax expense by $9,450 when the disposition occurs
Reduce income tax expense by $12,600 when the disposition occurs
No tax effect is recognized for ISOs
exp: No DTA is recorded for ISOs because no deduction is expected; when a disqualifying disposition creates a deduction, the benefit ($45,000 x 21% = $9,450) is recognized in income tax expense at that time. The $12,600 answer applies the rate to book compensation rather than the actual deduction.

q: Nolan Co.'s employees began working on an incentive project on February 1. The board approved a stock option award for them on March 1, but the key terms were not communicated to employees until June 30, four months later, which is not considered a relatively short time period. What is the grant date for ASC 718 purposes?
exp: The grant date is when the employer and employee reach a mutual understanding of the key terms and all approvals are obtained; with a four-month delay in communication, that is June 30. Service may begin before the grant date (February 1 is the service inception date), but that does not make it the grant date.

q: Oriel Inc., a nonpublic company, granted employee stock options. Oriel cannot reasonably estimate its own expected share-price volatility because it has no internal market for its shares and no reliable historical data. How should Oriel measure the options under ASC 718?
choices: At intrinsic value on the grant date with no remeasurement
At fair value using the volatility of the S&P 500 index
At calculated value, substituting the historical volatility of an appropriate industry sector index
Using the minimum value method, which assumes zero volatility
exp: A nonpublic entity that cannot estimate its own volatility uses calculated value, replacing its volatility with the historical volatility of an appropriate industry sector index (ASC 718-10-30-20). The minimum value method was eliminated, and a broad market index is not an appropriate sector index.

q: Pembrook Co. granted 2,000 shares of its stock to an outside consultant for services to be performed over one year. The grant-date fair value was $30 per share, and the price was $35 when the services were completed at year-end. Under current ASC 718, what cost should Pembrook recognize for the year?
exp: After ASU 2018-07, equity-classified nonemployee awards are measured at grant-date fair value, like employee awards: 2,000 x $30 = $60,000. The $70,000 answer uses the old measurement-date approach at service completion.

q: Quarry Corp. has 4,000 cash-settled SARs that are fully vested and outstanding. During the year, the fair value of each SAR fell from $9 to $6. What is the effect on compensation expense for the year?
choices: No effect, because vested awards are not remeasured
exp: Liability-classified awards are remeasured at fair value each reporting date until settlement, even after vesting, and the full change goes to compensation cost: 4,000 x ($9 - $6) = $12,000 reduction. Freezing the measurement at vesting is an equity-award concept.

q: Ridgeway Inc. granted 16,000 RSUs with a grant-date fair value of $25 each, cliff vesting in four years. Ridgeway's policy is to account for forfeitures as they occur. No RSUs were forfeited in Year 1; 1,600 were forfeited in Year 2. What compensation cost should Ridgeway recognize in Year 2?
exp: Year 1 cost was 16,000 x $25 / 4 = $100,000; cumulative cost through Year 2 is 14,400 x $25 x 2/4 = $180,000, so Year 2 cost is $80,000, reversing the Year 1 cost on the forfeited units. The $90,000 answer ignores the catch-up for forfeitures.

q: When measuring the grant-date fair value of employee stock options with an option-pricing model, which of the following changes in assumptions would decrease the option's fair value, all else equal?
exp: Dividends paid during the option term reduce the share price without benefiting the holder, so a higher expected dividend yield lowers call option value. Longer term, higher volatility, and a higher risk-free rate all increase the value of a call option.

q: Sterling Co. granted 5,000 options with a grant-date fair value of $8 that vest upon achieving a sales target. The target was improbable, so no cost was recognized. Sterling later modified the target, making vesting probable, when the modified options had a fair value of $6. What total compensation cost should Sterling recognize for the modified award?
exp: For an improbable-to-probable (Type III) modification, the original grant-date fair value is ignored and cost is based on the modification-date fair value: 5,000 x $6 = $30,000. Using the $8 original grant-date value applies probable-to-probable modification logic.

q: Thornton Inc. cancelled an unvested stock option award without offering any replacement award or other consideration. At the cancellation date, $45,000 of the award's grant-date fair value had not yet been recognized. How should Thornton account for the cancellation?
choices: Recognize the $45,000 of unrecognized cost immediately
Reverse all previously recognized compensation cost
Continue recognizing the $45,000 over the remaining original vesting period
exp: A cancellation without a concurrent replacement award is treated as a repurchase for no consideration, so any previously unrecognized compensation cost is recognized at the cancellation date (ASC 718-20-35-9). Reversing prior cost is the treatment for a forfeiture, which is a different event.

q: Underhill Corp. repurchased 1,000 vested employee stock options for $9 cash each when their fair value was $7 each. How much compensation cost should Underhill recognize at the repurchase date?
exp: Cash paid up to the fair value of the repurchased instruments ($7,000) is charged to equity; the $2,000 excess over fair value is additional compensation cost (ASC 718-20-35-7). Expensing the full $9,000 treats the entire payment as compensation.

q: Which of the following share-based payment awards granted by Vickers Co. to employees should be classified as a liability under ASC 718?
choices: Stock appreciation rights that must be settled in shares
RSUs net share settled, with shares withheld up to the maximum statutory tax rate
Options whose underlying shares employees may require Vickers to repurchase for cash at fair value within three months after exercise
Standard options that cliff vest after four years and are settled in shares
exp: Shares that can be put to the employer within six months of exercise or vesting cause the award to be classified as a liability (ASC 718-10-25-9). After ASU 2016-09, withholding up to the maximum statutory rate does not trigger liability classification, and share-settled SARs are equity.

q: When 1,000 of Whitman Co.'s RSUs vested at a share price of $50, Whitman withheld 370 shares to cover the employee's taxes and remitted $18,500 to the tax authority. How should the $18,500 be classified in Whitman's statement of cash flows?
choices: Noncash activity disclosed in the notes
exp: Cash paid to a tax authority when shares are withheld to meet statutory withholding is classified as a financing activity under ASC 230, because it is economically a repurchase of shares. Operating is tempting because it relates to compensation, but the guidance specifies financing.

q: Yates Corp. had 10,000 employee stock options outstanding all year with an exercise price of $20. The average market price of the stock for the year was $25, and the average unrecognized compensation cost for the options was $30,000. Using the treasury stock method, how many incremental shares are included in diluted EPS?
exp: Assumed proceeds include the exercise price plus average unrecognized compensation: $200,000 + $30,000 = $230,000, repurchasing 9,200 shares at $25, so 10,000 - 9,200 = 800 incremental shares. The 2,000 answer ignores unrecognized compensation in assumed proceeds.

q: Zimmer Inc.'s 2,000 vested cash-settled SARs, which had a carrying liability of $14,000 at the prior year-end, were exercised when the share price was $30. The SARs had a base price of $22. What compensation expense should Zimmer recognize on settlement?
exp: The settlement amount is 2,000 x ($30 - $22) = $16,000; since $14,000 was already accrued, the remaining $2,000 is recognized as compensation expense when the liability is remeasured to its settlement amount. The $16,000 answer double counts amounts already expensed.

q: Abernathy Co. granted 3,000 options vesting 1,000 at the end of each of the next three years. Abernathy valued each tranche separately: $4 for the one-year tranche, $5 for the two-year tranche, and $6 for the three-year tranche. Using accelerated (tranche-by-tranche) attribution, what compensation cost should Abernathy recognize in Year 1?
exp: Each tranche is attributed over its own service period: $4,000/1 + $5,000/2 + $6,000/3 = $4,000 + $2,500 + $2,000 = $8,500. The $5,000 answer spreads total cost straight-line, which is not the method described.

q: Beaumont Corp. granted an employee 1,000 options with a grant-date fair value of $10 and had recognized $6,000 of cost. When the employee was terminated before vesting, Beaumont modified the award to accelerate vesting; the modification-date fair value was $4 per option. What is the net effect on compensation cost at the modification date?
exp: Without the modification the award would have been forfeited, so this is an improbable-to-probable modification: the $6,000 previously recognized is reversed and the $4,000 modification-date fair value is recognized, a $2,000 net reduction. Recognizing only the $4,000 ignores the reversal of the original award's cost.

q: Calloway Inc. granted 6,000 stock appreciation rights that will be settled in shares of its stock, with a grant-date fair value of $8 each and a two-year cliff vesting period. At the end of Year 1, the fair value of each SAR was $10. What compensation cost should Calloway recognize in Year 1?
exp: Share-settled SARs are equity-classified, so cost is fixed at grant-date fair value: 6,000 x $8 / 2 = $24,000. The $30,000 answer remeasures at year-end fair value, which applies only to liability (cash-settled) awards.

q: Dorsey Co. granted plain-vanilla employee stock options with a 10-year contractual term that cliff vest after four years. Dorsey lacks sufficient historical exercise data and uses the simplified method to estimate expected term. What expected term should Dorsey use?
exp: The simplified method uses the average of the vesting term and the contractual term: (4 + 10) / 2 = 7 years. Using the 10-year contractual term ignores expected early exercise, which overstates option value.

q: Easton Co., a nonpublic entity, elected to measure its liability-classified awards at intrinsic value. It granted 1,000 cash-settled SARs with a base price of $10 that cliff vest in two years. At the end of Year 1, the share value was $16 and the SAR fair value was $9. What compensation cost should Easton recognize in Year 1?
exp: Under the nonpublic intrinsic value election, the liability is 1,000 x ($16 - $10) = $6,000, recognized pro rata for one of two years of service: $3,000. The $4,500 answer uses fair value rather than the elected intrinsic value.

q: Fletcher Corp. granted performance share units with a target of 10,000 units and a grant-date fair value of $20 per unit. Units earned range from 0% to 150% of target based on a three-year cumulative earnings goal. At the end of Year 1, Fletcher concluded that 120% achievement is probable. What compensation cost should Fletcher recognize in Year 1?
exp: Cost is based on the probable outcome of the performance condition: 10,000 x 120% x $20 = $240,000 total, recognized over three years, so $80,000 in Year 1. The $66,667 answer uses target (100%) rather than the probable 120% outcome.

q: Graham Co. recognized $200,000 of share-based compensation for the year. Of this amount, $50,000 related to employees who spent all their time building a manufacturing facility for Graham's own use. How much share-based compensation should Graham report as expense for the year?
exp: Share-based compensation is a cost of employee services and is capitalized when it relates to producing an asset, as with cash compensation: $200,000 - $50,000 capitalized = $150,000 expensed. Expensing all $200,000 ignores the capitalization of costs for self-constructed assets.

q: Harmon Inc. recognized $100,000 of compensation cost and a $21,000 deferred tax asset for nonqualified options. When the options were exercised, the intrinsic value deduction was only $70,000. The tax rate is 21%. How should the tax shortfall be recognized?
exp: The actual benefit is $70,000 x 21% = $14,700 versus the $21,000 DTA, leaving a $6,300 shortfall that increases income tax expense under ASU 2016-09. The $30,000 answer confuses the deduction shortfall with its tax effect, and charging APIC is the superseded treatment.

q: Irwin Co. granted 4,000 RSUs (fair value $25 each) to an executive who is already eligible for retirement. Under the award terms, the RSUs vest on a four-year schedule but continue to vest in full if the executive retires, so no further service is required to earn them. How should Irwin recognize the compensation cost?
choices: $50,000 in each of the first two years
exp: The requisite service period ends when the employee is no longer required to provide service to earn the award; because the executive is already retirement-eligible, the full 4,000 x $25 = $100,000 is recognized at grant. Spreading the cost over the nominal four-year schedule ignores that no service is actually required.

q: Jennings Corp. had 10,000 employee stock options outstanding all year with an exercise price of $30. The average market price of Jennings's stock was $28, and the options have no unrecognized compensation cost. How many incremental shares should be included in diluted EPS?
exp: Options whose exercise price exceeds the average market price are antidilutive: proceeds of $300,000 would repurchase about 10,714 shares, more than the 10,000 issued, so no incremental shares are included. Including all 10,000 shares ignores the treasury stock method.

q: Kingsley Co. granted incentive stock options and recognized $80,000 of compensation cost this year. The tax rate is 21%, and no disqualifying dispositions are expected. What deferred tax asset should Kingsley recognize for the options?
exp: Incentive stock options generally do not produce a tax deduction for the employer, so no deferred tax asset is recorded unless a disqualifying disposition occurs. $16,800 (21% of $80,000) would be right for nonqualified options.

q: Linden Inc. granted 1,000 options each to 50 employees, with a grant-date fair value of $15 per option and three-year cliff vesting. Linden's policy is to estimate forfeitures, and it expects 8% of the options to be forfeited. What compensation cost should Linden recognize in Year 1, assuming no change in estimate?
exp: Expected cost is 50,000 options x 92% x $15 = $690,000, recognized over three years: $230,000 per year. The $250,000 answer ignores estimated forfeitures, which Linden's policy requires.
